# Reshape tables

## A small tibble to practise on

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
#| label: yearly
library(tidyverse)

yearly <- tibble(
  act_use_cat = c("S/F Res", "S/F Res",
                  "S/F Res", "S/F Res",
                  "Strata Res", "Strata Res",
                  "Strata Res", "Strata Res"),
  sale_year = c(2022, 2023, 2024, 2025,
                2022, 2023, 2024, 2025),
  avg_price = c(2000000, 1900000, 1850000, 1800000,
                800000, 800000, 780000, 800000)
)
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
```{r}
#| label: yearly-print
yearly
```
:::
::::

Average prices by type and year. One row per type **and** year: a **long** table.

## How would you compute the ratio?

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="44%"}
```{r}
#| label: ratio-data
yearly
```
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
Compute the ratio of the single-family price to the strata price in each year. The result should look like this:

```{r}
#| label: ratio-target
#| echo: false
yearly |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = act_use_cat, values_from = avg_price) |>
  mutate(ratio = `S/F Res` / `Strata Res`) |>
  select(sale_year, ratio)
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
- Students who remember deck 05 may write `group_by(sale_year) |> summarise(ratio = avg_price[act_use_cat == "S/F Res"] / avg_price[act_use_cat == "Strata Res"])`. It works. The next slide is shorter and keeps both prices beside the ratio.
:::

## Answer: make the table wide, then divide

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{r}
#| label: wider
wide <- yearly |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = act_use_cat,
              values_from = avg_price)
wide
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| label: ratio
wide |>
  mutate(ratio = `S/F Res` / `Strata Res`)
```
:::
::::

- `names_from`: the column whose values become the new column names. `values_from`: the column that fills them. Every other column, here `sale_year`, decides the rows.
- Each type is now a column, so the ratio is one `mutate()`. `S/F Res` is not a valid R name, so it needs backticks; without them, R reads `S/F` as S divided by F.

## Can you draw this chart?

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="44%"}
```{r}
#| label: chart-data
wide
```
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
```{r}
#| label: chart-target
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.8
ggplot(yearly, aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_line()
```
:::
::::

Suppose you have only `wide`, as when a download comes wide. Write code that draws this chart from it.

::: {.notes}
- If students are stuck: which column would `colour =` map? `wide` has none that holds the type.
:::

## Answer: make the table long, then plot

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: longer
#| fig-show: hide
long <- wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(`S/F Res`, `Strata Res`),
               names_to = "act_use_cat",
               values_to = "avg_price")

ggplot(long, aes(sale_year, avg_price,
                 colour = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_line()
```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: longer-print
long
```
:::
::::

- `cols` lists the columns to stack. `names_to` and `values_to` name the two new columns, in quotes because they do not exist yet.
- `colour =` needs one column that holds the type. From `wide`, you would need one `geom_line()` per column, and get no legend.

::: {.notes}
- The wide version: `` ggplot(wide, aes(x = sale_year)) + geom_line(aes(y = `S/F Res`)) + geom_line(aes(y = `Strata Res`)) ``. Two layers, no legend, and the y-axis is named `S/F Res`, after the first layer.
- `cols = -sale_year` does the same: every column except `sale_year`.
- `long` holds the same rows as `yearly`, in a different order.
:::

## Extra columns split the rows

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{r}
#| label: split-data
yearly_n <- yearly |>
  mutate(n_sales = c(2, 3, 1, 4, 5, 2, 6, 3))
yearly_n
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| label: split
yearly_n |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = act_use_cat,
              values_from = avg_price)
```
:::
::::

::: {.warning}
No warning, but eight rows with gaps: `n_sales` also decides the rows. Keep only the columns you need: `select(sale_year, act_use_cat, avg_price)`.
:::

::: {.notes}
- `id_cols = sale_year` inside `pivot_wider()` does the same as the `select()`.
- `values_fill = 0` fills gaps where a missing combination means zero, such as an area with no strata sales in a table of counts.
- Two values for the same cell, such as two rows for strata in 2025, are a different problem. R warns, and the cells become lists (`<list>`). Find them with `count(sale_year, act_use_cat) |> filter(n > 1)`.
:::

## Quick check: what is wrong with this chart?

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: renters-w
renters_w <- tibble(city = c("Vancouver", "Surrey"),
                    `2001` = c(56, 26), `2006` = c(52, 25), `2016` = c(53, 28), `2021` = c(55, 31))
```
:::

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| label: renters
#| fig-show: hide
renters <- renters_w |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -city, names_to = "year",
               values_to = "renter_pct")
ggplot(renters, aes(year, renter_pct,
                    colour = city)) +
  geom_point()
```
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
```{r}
#| label: renters-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 2.8
ggplot(renters, aes(year, renter_pct, colour = city)) +
  geom_point()
```
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
The years are evenly spaced, so 2006 sits as close to 2016 as to 2001. `names_to` makes `year` text, and ggplot spaces text as categories. Add `mutate(year = as.numeric(year))` after the pivot.
:::

::: {.notes}
- The renter shares are made up. 2011 is missing on purpose: the 2011 long-form census was the voluntary National Household Survey, which analysts often leave out.
- With `geom_line()` instead of `geom_point()`, the chart is empty, with the message "Each group consists of only one observation": text on the x-axis makes each year its own group.
:::

## Practice: the single-family premium

```{r}
#| label: bca
bca <- read_rds("data/bca262.rds")
```

Using `bca`, for the City of Vancouver from 2016 to 2025:

1. compute the median price of each `act_use_cat` in each year;
2. make the table wide, with one column per type;
3. add the ratio of the single-family median to the strata median.

In which year was the ratio highest?

## Answer

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: premium
premium <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", year(sale_date) %in% 2016:2025) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat, sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(median_price = median(price, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = act_use_cat, values_from = median_price) |>
  mutate(ratio = `S/F Res` / `Strata Res`) |>
  arrange(desc(ratio))
premium |> head(4)
```
:::

In `r premium$sale_year[1]`, a single-family home cost `r round(premium$ratio[1], 1)` times a strata home. In 2025, the ratio was `r round(premium$ratio[premium$sale_year == 2025], 1)`.

::: {.notes}
- A student who also computes `n()` in `summarise()` will get 20 rows with gaps: the extra-columns trap.
:::

# Join tables

## Two tables that share a column

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: sales
sales <- tibble(
  sale_id = 1:4,
  neigh = c("Kitsilano", "Oakridge",
            "Kitsilano", "Dunbar-Southlands"),
  price = c(1250000, 1400000,
            980000, 2100000)
)
sales
```
:::

::: {.column width="43%"}
```{r}
#| label: area-info
area_info <- tibble(
  neigh = c("Kitsilano", "Oakridge",
            "West End"),
  skytrain = c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
area_info
```
:::
::::

A **join** adds the columns of one table to another, matching rows by a **key**: here `neigh`. `skytrain` says whether the local area has a SkyTrain station.

## left_join() keeps every row of the left table

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="44%"}
```{r}
#| label: left-data
sales
area_info
```
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
```{r}
#| label: left
sales |>
  left_join(area_info, by = "neigh")
```
:::
::::

Four sales in, four rows out. Dunbar-Southlands has no row in `area_info`, so its `skytrain` is `NA`. West End has no sale, so it does not appear.

## inner_join() keeps only the rows that match

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="44%"}
```{r}
#| label: inner-data
sales
area_info
```
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
```{r}
#| label: inner
sales |>
  inner_join(area_info, by = "neigh")
```

::: {.warning}
Four sales in, three rows out: the Dunbar-Southlands sale is gone, with no message. Use `left_join()` unless you mean to drop the rows without a match.
:::
:::
::::

## Which rows does each join keep?

| Code | Keeps |
|---|---|
| `left_join(x, y)` | Every row of `x`, with `NA` where `y` has no match |
| `inner_join(x, y)` | Only the rows of `x` with a match in `y` |
| `full_join(x, y)` | Every row of both tables |
| `right_join(x, y)` | Every row of `y` |

Each join adds the columns of `y` to `x`. They differ only in which rows they keep.

::: {.notes}
- `sales |> full_join(area_info, by = "neigh")` gives five rows: the four sales and West End, with `NA` for `sale_id` and `price`.
- `right_join(x, y)` is `left_join(y, x)` with the columns in a different order. It is rare in practice.
:::

## Keys can have different names

```{r}
#| label: stations
stations <- tibble(
  station = c("Oakridge - 41st Avenue", "Langara - 49th Avenue", "Marine Drive"),
  geo_local_area = c("Oakridge", "Oakridge", "Marpole")
)
```

The City of Vancouver's station data call the local area `geo_local_area`. Name both columns with `join_by()`, the left table's first:

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: join-by
sales |>
  left_join(stations, by = join_by(neigh == geo_local_area))
```
:::

## A duplicate key adds rows

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
#| label: dup-rows
nrow(sales)
sales |>
  left_join(stations,
            by = join_by(neigh == geo_local_area)) |>
  nrow()
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
Check the key before you join:

```{r}
#| label: dup-check
stations |>
  count(geo_local_area) |>
  filter(n > 1)
```
:::
::::

Oakridge has two stations, so its sale matched twice. Any average or count over the joined rows now counts it twice.

## relationship = makes R check for you

```{r}
#| label: relationship
sales |>
  left_join(stations, by = join_by(neigh == geo_local_area),
            relationship = "many-to-one")
```

`"many-to-one"`: many sales may share a key, but each key may appear only once in `stations`. The silent duplicate becomes an error.

::: {.notes}
- Without `relationship =`, dplyr warns only when keys repeat in **both** tables ("many-to-many"). A key that repeats in one table adds rows silently.
- `"one-to-one"` also requires each key to appear only once in the left table.
:::

## Predict the output

```{r}
#| label: predict-code
#| eval: false
sales |>
  inner_join(stations, by = join_by(neigh == geo_local_area))
```

How many rows, and which sales?

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| label: predict-out
#| echo: false
sales |>
  inner_join(stations, by = join_by(neigh == geo_local_area))
```

Two rows, both sale 2. Kitsilano and Dunbar-Southlands have no station, so the inner join drops three sales. Oakridge has two stations, so sale 2 appears twice.
:::

## anti_join() finds the rows that did not match

```{r}
#| label: anti
sales |>
  anti_join(area_info, by = "neigh")
```

`anti_join(x, y)` returns the rows of `x` with no match in `y`, and only the columns of `x`. Run it before an `inner_join()` to see what you will drop, and after a `left_join()` to see which rows got `NA`.

::: {.key-point}
After every join, check both directions: rows that matched twice (`relationship =`) and rows that did not match (`anti_join()`). A row count alone can miss them when they cancel out.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Deck 08 uses `anti_join()` on real data: most of BC Assessment's neighbourhood names have no City local area of the same name.
:::

# Application: repeat sales

## A repeat sale compares a home with itself

```{r}
#| label: repeat-data
van <- bca |> filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver")

sales_2015 <- van |>
  filter(year(sale_date) == 2015) |>
  select(folioid, act_use_cat, price_2015 = price)

sales_2025 <- van |>
  filter(year(sale_date) == 2025) |>
  select(folioid, price_2025 = price)
```

- In deck 05, an average fell while every type rose, because the mix of homes sold changed. Comparing each home with its own earlier price avoids the mix.
- `folioid` identifies a property. In `bca`, it starts in 2015.
- `select(price_2015 = price)` keeps `price` under a new name. If both tables kept `price`, the join would return `price.x` and `price.y`.

## Practice: how much did the same homes gain?

Join `sales_2015` and `sales_2025` so that only homes sold in both years remain.

1. Before you join, check that `folioid` appears only once in each table.
2. After you join, compute for each `act_use_cat` the number of homes and the median of `price_2025 / price_2015 - 1`.

::: {.fragment}
Hint, if a `folioid` appears more than once: `group_by(folioid) |> filter(n() == 1) |> ungroup()` keeps the homes sold once that year.
:::

## Answer: check the keys

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: repeat-keys
sales_2015 |> count(folioid) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()
sales_2025 |> count(folioid) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()
```

```{r}
#| label: flip-gap
#| include: false
flip_days <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", year(sale_date) == 2015) |>
  group_by(folioid) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>
  summarise(days = as.numeric(max(sale_date) - min(sale_date)))
```

Some homes sold twice in one year. Joined as they are, a home sold twice in 2015 and twice in 2025 would become four rows. Keep the homes sold once in each year:

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: repeat-once
once_2015 <- sales_2015 |> group_by(folioid) |> filter(n() == 1) |> ungroup()
once_2025 <- sales_2025 |> group_by(folioid) |> filter(n() == 1) |> ungroup()
```

::: {.notes}
- Most of the 2015 resales came a few months after the first sale: the median gap is `r round(median(flip_days$days))` days.
- Dropping them is a choice, and it should be stated. Keeping the last 2015 sale and the first 2025 sale is another.
- `relationship = "one-to-one"` on the next slide would stop the join if any duplicate were left.
:::

## Answer: join and summarise

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: repeat-join
repeat_sales <- once_2015 |>
  inner_join(once_2025, by = "folioid", relationship = "one-to-one")
nrow(repeat_sales)

repeat_sales |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  summarise(homes = n(), median_growth = median(price_2025 / price_2015 - 1))
```
:::

Of `r scales::comma(nrow(sales_2015))` sales in 2015, `r nrow(repeat_sales)` homes sold again, once, in 2025.

```{r}
#| label: rebuilt
#| include: false
rebuilt <- bca |>
  filter(folioid %in% repeat_sales$folioid, act_use_cat == "S/F Res",
         year(sale_date) %in% c(2015, 2025)) |>
  group_by(folioid) |>
  summarise(rebuilt = n_distinct(year_built, na.rm = TRUE) > 1)
```

::: {.notes}
- `r sum(rebuilt$rebuilt)` of the `r nrow(rebuilt)` houses have a different `year_built` in 2025: a new house on the old lot. Their price change includes the construction.
- One house "fell" 98%: its 2025 price is $17,420, which is not a market sale. The median is not affected.
:::

## Same homes, a different story

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: all-sales
all_sales <- van |>
  filter(year(sale_date) %in% c(2015, 2025)) |>
  group_by(act_use_cat, sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(median_price = median(price), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sale_year, values_from = median_price) |>
  mutate(growth = `2025` / `2015` - 1)
all_sales
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: compare-numbers
#| include: false
pct <- \(x) round(100 * x)
all_g <- set_names(all_sales$growth, all_sales$act_use_cat)
rep_g <- repeat_sales |>
  group_by(act_use_cat) |>
  summarise(g = median(price_2025 / price_2015 - 1)) |>
  deframe()
```

::: {.key-point}
All sales: strata prices rose `r pct(all_g[["Strata Res"]])`%, single-family `r pct(all_g[["S/F Res"]])`%. The same homes: `r pct(rep_g[["Strata Res"]])`% and `r pct(rep_g[["S/F Res"]])`%. Different homes sold in each year. Neither is *the* price change: repeat sales are a small, selected group, and some houses were rebuilt in between.
:::
